h1: Setting up a nano brewery and what it can realistically earn
title: Nano Brewery: Set-Up and What It Earns | Craft Beer School
desc: What a nano brewery is, what it costs to run and a worked example of revenue, costs and profit. Use your own numbers before you commit.
teaser: A nano brewery is cheap to start and small to earn from. The arithmetic is worth doing before you sign a lease.
standfirst: A nano brewery lets you start small, learn fast and keep risk low. It also caps how much you can earn. Here is a worked example with made up numbers and the method for replacing them with yours.
sections: What counts as a nano brewery

There is no single legal definition. In practice, a nano brewery has a brewhouse of a few hundred litres at most, often 100 to 500 litres, with a handful of fermenters and a small cold room. One or two people run it. Some sell from a tiny taproom. Others package for local shops and bars. Many do a bit of both.

Whether a state licence exists for a business that small varies. Some states license by brewery type or capacity. Fees and conditions differ. Our guide to pouring craft beer without a brewery in Maharashtra shows one alternative route. Ask the state excise office or a licensing adviser what fits a very small operation.

Revenue is limited by how much beer you can make and sell. Start with capacity.

Here is an illustration. The numbers are made up, so replace them with your own. A 200 litre brewhouse brewing two batches a week for 50 weeks produces 20,000 litres a year. Allow 8% for losses in transfers, yeast, trub and packaging. That leaves 18,400 litres to sell.

At an average price of ₹250 a litre, revenue is ₹46,00,000. If ingredients, packaging, gas, water, cleaning chemicals and excise-related costs add up to ₹90 a litre, the variable cost is ₹16,56,000. Contribution is ₹29,44,000.
The fixed costs that eat it

Fixed costs do not move with volume. Rent, power, licence fees, insurance, equipment finance, accounting, marketing and wages are all on the list. In our illustration, suppose they total ₹25,00,000 a year. That includes a modest wage for the owner-brewer.

Profit before tax and before any loan repayment is ₹29,44,000 minus ₹25,00,000, or ₹4,44,000. That is a thin cushion. A drop of just 10% in volume, from 18,400 to 16,560 litres, takes contribution to ₹26,49,600 and profit to ₹1,49,600. A nano brewery runs close to its break-even most of the year.

Three levers move profit more than the rest.

  • Price per litre. Selling in your own taproom earns far more per litre than selling kegs to a bar.
  • Losses. Each point of loss is beer you paid to make and cannot sell, so measure yield at every transfer.
  • Utilisation. A brewery that sits idle three days a week carries its fixed costs on fewer litres.

Test each lever on your spreadsheet. Raise the price by ₹20, cut losses by 3 points and add one extra batch a month. Then look at the result.
Water, power and the small stuff

At a small scale, utilities become a visible cost. Craft breweries commonly use several litres of water for every litre of beer, so measure your own. A borewell or municipal supply may need treatment. Drainage and effluent rules apply. Our guide to rainwater harvesting at a brewery shows what it can and cannot supply.

Cooling matters in India. A glycol chiller and an insulated cold room cost money, yet fermentation temperature and beer cold storage decide quality in a hot climate. Do not cut that corner.

Capacity means nothing until the beer is sold. Decide in advance where the 18,400 litres will go: your own taproom, kegs to bars, cans or bottles to shops, events. Each route has a different price, a different cost to serve and different licence conditions. A route that takes half your time for a tenth of your revenue is a hobby, not a business. Track the contribution per route every month.

A very small company still benefits from advice. Think about who will check your accounts, who understands excise, who knows food safety and who can tell you honestly whether the beer is good. Our guide to setting up a board and advisers for a small brewery company explains how to build that circle without much cost.

A nano brewery suits someone who wants to learn the craft, test a brand or run a taproom with a personal feel. It does not suit someone who needs a large income quickly. If your numbers show a thin profit, you can raise volume with a bigger brewhouse, but that adds capital and risk. Work the figures for two sizes before deciding.

This is where costing, cash flow and break-even analysis matter most. They are what we teach in the Brewery Business Management course.
faqs: How much beer can a nano brewery make?
A 200 litre brewhouse brewing two batches a week makes roughly 20,000 litres a year before losses. Replace the numbers with your own batch size and schedule.
It can be, but margins are often thin because fixed costs are spread over few litres. Work out your break-even volume before you commit.
Does a nano brewery need a licence?
Yes. Alcohol production and sale need permission. Categories and fees vary by state. Check with the excise office or a licensing adviser.
